title: Jump Game VI
statement:
You start on index `0` of the integer array `nums` (length `n`) and must finish on index `n - 1`. Each jump moves you forward by between `1` and `k` positions and must land inside the array, so from index `i` you may land on any index from `i + 1` to `min(n - 1, i + k)`.

Your score is the total of `nums[j]` over every index `j` you stand on, counting both the starting and the final index. Return the largest score any sequence of jumps can achieve.
notes:
## Intuition

Let `best[i]` be the highest score of any path that ends on index `i`. The last jump into `i` came from one of the `k` indices before it, so `best[i] = nums[i] + max(best[i - k .. i - 1])`. Scanning those `k` values every time is O(n·k), too slow when both are large (trying every path is exponential).

The window of candidates slides one step right per index, so this is a sliding-window maximum. A deque of indices whose `best` values strictly decrease from front to back keeps the window's maximum at the front at all times.

## Approach

1. Set `best[0] = nums[0]` and put index 0 in `deque`; `head` marks the deque's live front.
2. For each later index `i`, advance `head` past indices smaller than `i - k`: they are too far back to jump from.
3. The front index now holds the window's largest score, so `best[i] = nums[i] + best[deque[head]]`.
4. Pop indices from the back while their score is at most `best[i]`: `i` is newer and at least as good, so they can never be the maximum again.
5. Push `i`. After the loop, return `best[n - 1]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, -1, -2, 4, -7, 3]`, `k = 2`.

- `best[0] = 1`, deque `[0]`.
- `i = 1`: `best[1] = -1 + 1 = 0`; deque `[0, 1]`.
- `i = 2`: `best[2] = -2 + 1 = -1`; deque `[0, 1, 2]`.
- `i = 3`: index 0 leaves the window; front is 1, so `best[3] = 4 + 0 = 4`; it pops 2 and 1, deque `[3]`.
- `i = 4`: `best[4] = -7 + 4 = -3`; deque `[3, 4]`.
- `i = 5`: front 3 is still in range, `best[5] = 3 + 4 = 7`.

The answer is `7` (path `1, -1, 4, 3`).

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each index is pushed once and leaves the deque at most once.
- Space: O(n) for `best` and the deque.

## Pitfalls

- Greedily jumping to the largest reachable value fails: a big value now can strand you before a long run of large negatives.
- Expire indices below `i - k`, not `i - k - 1`: from index `i - k` the jump of length `k` is still allowed.
- `k` may exceed the array length; the window simply covers every earlier index.
- Using `Array.prototype.shift` for the front makes each removal O(n); a moving `head` index keeps it O(1).

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `best` | `best[i]` is the top score of a path ending on index `i` |
| `deque` | indices with decreasing `best`, oldest at the front |
| `head` | position of the live front inside `deque` |
| `i` | the index being scored |

narration.3: best[i] will hold the highest score of any path that ends on index i.
narration.4: A path ending on index 0 is just the starting square.
narration.5: The deque holds candidate indices to jump from, with decreasing scores.
narration.6: head points at the live front of the deque; earlier slots are discarded.
narration.8: Score every later index from left to right.
narration.9: The front index is too far back if it is smaller than i - k.
narration.10: Discard it so the front is a legal place to jump from.
narration.12: Jump from the front index, the reachable one with the highest score.
narration.13: Indices at the back scoring no more than best[i] can never be the best again.
narration.16: Add i as a candidate for the next k indices.
narration.18: The best path that ends on the last index is the answer.
